chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks

questions.question: What three topics does the 'This chapter covers' box list for chapter 2?
questions.answer: A first example of a neural network; tensors and tensor operations; how neural networks learn via backpropagation and gradient descent.
questions.explanation: These are the three bullets printed in the chapter-opener box.

questions.question: According to the authors, what is the most precise, unambiguous description of a mathematical operation?
options: Its executable code
Its formal mathematical notation
A diagram
A worked numerical example
questions.answer: Its executable code
questions.explanation: The page states this directly, as the justification for steering away from mathematical notation. Diagrams and numerical examples are aids the book also uses, but the authors name code as the precise description.

questions.question: Why does the chapter start with a practical neural-network example before explaining tensors and gradient descent?
questions.answer: To provide sufficient context: the example introduces the concepts concretely, and the chapter then goes over every new concept point by point.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph gives this plan explicitly and warns that the concepts are essential for the practical examples in later chapters.

questions.question: Which four mathematical notions does the opener name, and in which sections of chapter 2 are they developed?
questions.answer: Tensors (section 2.2, p.45), tensor operations (2.3, p.52), differentiation and gradient descent (2.4, p.63).
questions.explanation: The first paragraph lists 'tensors, tensor operations, differentiation, gradient descent, and so on'; the chapter outline maps them to sections 2.2–2.4.

questions.question: Before reading on: can you already say in one sentence what a tensor is and what gradient descent does? Write your current answers down and compare them with the chapter's definitions on p.45 and p.63 later.
questions.answer: Open-ended; the chapter will define a tensor as a multidimensional array of numbers and gradient descent as iteratively moving parameters against the gradient of the loss.
questions.explanation: A chapter opener is the right moment to record prior intuitions so you can see what the chapter changes.

questions.question: How many images does MNIST contain, and how are they divided?
options: 60,000 training images and 10,000 test images
50,000 training images and 10,000 test images
60,000 images in total, with no fixed split
70,000 training images and 7,000 test images
questions.answer: 60,000 training images and 10,000 test images
questions.explanation: The page states 'a set of 60,000 training images, plus 10,000 test images'. The total is 70,000, but it is split as 60k/10k, not 50k/10k or 70k/7k, and the split is fixed.

questions.question: Describe the classification problem of section 2.1 in one sentence, including the input format and the number of classes.
questions.answer: Classify grayscale images of handwritten digits, 28 × 28 pixels each, into 10 categories (the digits 0 through 9).
questions.explanation: All three elements — grayscale 28 × 28 input, 10 classes, digits 0–9 — are given verbatim on the page.

questions.question: What does the sidebar say is 'by far the easiest way' to run the book's notebooks?
options: Google Colaboratory (Colab)
A local machine with a GPU
The liveBook website
A plain Python script run from the terminal
questions.answer: Google Colaboratory (Colab)
questions.explanation: The sidebar names Colab as the easiest setup and the industry standard, with the notebooks defaulting to its free GPU runtime. Local execution is offered as an alternative, not the easiest route; the other options are not mentioned as ways to run the notebooks.

questions.question: Why do the authors call MNIST the 'Hello World' of deep learning?
questions.answer: Because solving it is what you do to verify that your algorithms are working as expected — a small, well-studied, universally known check rather than a demonstration of capability — and it appears over and over in papers and blog posts.
questions.explanation: The page gives the verification purpose explicitly; the analogy to a 'Hello World' program is about confirming the pipeline works, not about the difficulty of the task.

questions.question: What do the letters NIST in MNIST stand for, and when was the dataset assembled?
questions.answer: The National Institute of Standards and Technology; the dataset was assembled in the 1980s.
questions.explanation: The page says the images were 'assembled by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (the NIST in MNIST) in the 1980s'.

questions.question: The authors say some steps of the first example may 'look like magic'. What should the reader do about that, according to the page and the chapter plan on p.40?
questions.answer: Not worry: the following sections (2.2–2.5) review each element of the example and explain it in detail, so the reader should follow the gist now and expect the explanations to come point by point.
questions.explanation: The page says 'That's fine. In a few sections, we'll review each element in the example and explain it in detail', matching the example-first plan announced on the chapter opener.

questions.question: Have you opened the chapter 2 notebook (on Colab or locally) and confirmed that it runs? If not, do so before reading p.42, so you can execute each listing as it appears.
questions.answer: Open-ended; the goal is a working environment, per the sidebar's advice that you gain much more by running the code as you read.
questions.explanation: The sidebar's central recommendation is practical: run and experiment with the code.

questions.question: What is the shape of `train_images` immediately after Listing 2.1?
questions.explanation: The interactive session prints `(60000, 28, 28)`: 60,000 images of 28 × 28 pixels, samples axis first. (60000, 784) is the shape only after the reshape on p.44; (28, 28, 60000) puts the samples axis last, which NumPy/Keras do not do; (10000, 28, 28) is the test set.

questions.question: Define class, sample and label, and give the MNIST instance of each.
questions.answer: A class is a category in a classification problem (a digit 0–9); a sample is a data point (one 28 × 28 image); a label is the class associated with a specific sample (the digit that image shows).
questions.explanation: These are the definitions in the page's first NOTE, instantiated on the dataset loaded in Listing 2.1.

questions.question: According to the NOTE, why is NumPy rarely used to implement modern machine learning algorithms?
options: It lacks GPU and autodifferentiation support.
It cannot store integer arrays.
It is not compatible with Keras.
It is too slow to load datasets.
questions.answer: It lacks GPU and autodifferentiation support.
questions.explanation: The NOTE gives exactly these two missing capabilities. NumPy stores integer arrays (the labels are uint8), Keras accepts NumPy arrays directly (Listing 2.1), and loading speed is not mentioned.

questions.question: What does `len(train_labels)` return and why must it equal `train_images.shape[0]`?
questions.answer: 60000. Images and labels have a one-to-one correspondence: each of the 60,000 images has exactly one label, so the labels array must have one entry per sample along the images' first axis.
questions.explanation: The page prints `len(train_labels)` → 60000 and states that images and labels correspond one-to-one.

questions.question: Describe the example's workflow and explain the role of `test_labels` in it.
questions.answer: First the network is fed `train_images` and `train_labels` and learns to associate images with labels; then it produces predictions for `test_images`; finally those predictions are verified against `test_labels`. The test labels are used only for verification, never for learning.
questions.explanation: The workflow paragraph (continued on p.43) describes train → predict → verify; keeping the test labels out of training is what makes the verification meaningful.

questions.question: What are the first three and last three values of `train_labels` as printed, and what is their dtype?
questions.answer: 5, 0, 4 … 5, 6, 8; dtype uint8 (unsigned 8-bit integers).
questions.explanation: The session shows `array([5, 0, 4, ..., 5, 6, 8], dtype=uint8)`; NumPy abbreviates the middle with `...`.

questions.question: In your notebook, run Listing 2.1 and then display `train_images[0]` as an image and print `train_labels[0]`. Does the picture match the label (it should be a 5)?
questions.answer: Open-ended; `train_labels[0]` is 5 per the printed array, and the first image should show a handwritten 5.
questions.explanation: This checks the one-to-one correspondence between images and labels described on the page, using the interactive style the chapter encourages.

questions.question: In Listing 2.2, what does the argument `512` in `layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")` specify?
options: The number of input pixels of each MNIST image
The number of units (output dimensions) of the layer
The number of training images processed per batch
The number of digit classes
questions.answer: The number of units (output dimensions) of the layer
questions.explanation: The first positional argument of `Dense` is the number of units, i.e. the size of the representation the layer outputs. The input size (784 pixels) is inferred later; the batch size is set in `fit()` on p.44; and the number of classes (10) is the size of the *second* layer.

questions.question: Why does the last layer have exactly 10 units and a softmax activation?
questions.answer: Because there are 10 digit classes and softmax turns the 10 scores into probabilities that sum to 1, one per class.
questions.explanation: The page calls it a '10-way softmax classification layer' returning 'an array of 10 probability scores (summing to 1)', each the probability that the image belongs to one of the 10 digit classes.

questions.question: Explain the authors' description of a layer as a 'filter' and of a model as a 'sieve'. What is being filtered, and what does 'progressive data distillation' mean?
questions.answer: A layer takes data in and outputs a representation that is more useful for the task; chaining layers refines the representation step by step, so the information relevant to the problem is progressively concentrated (distilled) while irrelevant detail is left behind, like material passing through a succession of finer sieves.
questions.explanation: The page says layers 'extract representations out of the data fed into them—hopefully, representations that are more meaningful for the problem at hand', and that deep learning chains simple layers into 'a form of progressive data distillation'.

questions.question: Which of the three compile ingredients does NOT influence how the weights are updated during training?
options: The loss function
The optimizer
The metrics
All three influence the weight updates
questions.answer: The metrics
questions.explanation: Metrics are 'to monitor during training and testing'; they are reported, not optimized. The loss is what the model uses to 'steer itself in the right direction', and the optimizer is 'the mechanism through which the model will update itself'.

questions.question: Once the input is flattened to 784 values (p.44), how many learnable parameters does the model of Listing 2.2 have? Show the computation.
questions.answer: 784*512 + 512 = 401,920 for the first layer; 512*10 + 10 = 5,130 for the second; total 407,050.
questions.explanation: A Dense layer has a weight matrix of shape (inputs, units) plus one bias per unit, so its parameter count is inputs*units + units. Adding both layers gives 407,050. (The formula comes from the Dense computation `dot(input, W) + b` spelled out on p.76.)

questions.question: What does `optimizer="adam"` in Listing 2.3 do, in the terms used on this page?
questions.answer: It selects the optimizer, i.e. the mechanism through which the model will update itself based on the training data it sees, to improve its performance.
questions.explanation: The page defines the optimizer bullet exactly this way; `"adam"` names one particular optimizer (a variant of stochastic gradient descent, covered from p.63).

questions.question: Without looking, write Listing 2.2 from memory, then list the three things that must be chosen at compilation and one sentence on the role of each.
questions.answer: `model = keras.Sequential([layers.Dense(512, activation="relu"), layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")])`; loss function (measures performance to steer learning), optimizer (updates the weights), metrics (monitored, here accuracy).
questions.explanation: Self-check: if you could not reproduce the two Dense layers and the three compile ingredients, reread the listing and the bullet list on this page.

questions.question: After Listing 2.4, what are the shape and dtype of `train_images`?
questions.explanation: The page says the array is transformed from (60000, 28, 28) uint8 into a float32 array of shape (60000, 28 * 28) = (60000, 784). The samples axis stays first; the cast to float32 precedes the division by 255.

questions.question: Why is `astype("float32")` applied before `/ 255`, and what range do the values end up in?
questions.answer: So that the division is floating-point rather than integer arithmetic; the values end up in [0, 1].
questions.explanation: The book states the goal: 'scaling it so that all values are in the [0, 1] interval' and converting to a float32 array. Dividing a uint8 array directly would not produce the intended float32 fractions.

questions.question: With 60,000 training images, `batch_size=128` and `epochs=5`, how many weight updates does `fit()` perform?
questions.answer: ceil(60000/128) = 469 updates per epoch, times 5 epochs = 2,345 updates.
questions.explanation: Each batch yields one gradient update; 60000/128 = 468.75 so the last batch is partial and there are 469 per epoch. Section 2.5 (p.76) states these exact numbers.

questions.question: In Listing 2.6, what does `predictions[0]` contain?
options: The predicted digit for the first test image
Ten probabilities, one per digit class, for the first test image
The 784 pixel values of the first test image
The accuracy of the model on the first ten test images
questions.answer: Ten probabilities, one per digit class, for the first test image
questions.explanation: The page says each number of index i corresponds to the probability that `test_digits[0]` belongs to class i. The predicted digit requires an argmax (p.45); the pixels are in `test_digits[0]`; accuracy comes from `evaluate()` on p.45.

questions.question: The model reaches 0.989 accuracy during `fit()`. Why should you not conclude it will classify 98.9 % of new digits correctly?
questions.answer: Because that accuracy is measured on the training data the model learned from; performance on never-before-seen data is usually lower (97.8 % on the test set, p.45), a gap called overfitting.
questions.explanation: The page explicitly says the two displayed quantities are 'over the training data'. The next page compares with test accuracy and names the gap overfitting.

questions.question: What do the two keyword arguments `epochs=5` and `batch_size=128` in Listing 2.5 control?
questions.answer: `epochs=5`: the model passes over the entire training set five times; `batch_size=128`: the weights are updated after every group of 128 samples.
questions.explanation: This is the meaning given on p.76 ('iterate on the training data in mini-batches of 128 samples, 5 times over'); the page itself introduces the call as fitting the model to its training data.

questions.question: Could you write Listings 2.4 to 2.6 from memory and explain the purpose of each line to a classmate? Can you say why the test images must be preprocessed identically to the training images?
questions.answer: Reshape to (n, 784), cast to float32 and divide by 255 for both sets; fit for 5 epochs with batches of 128; slice ten test digits, predict, read the argmax. The test images must match the training preprocessing because the model's weights were learned for flat [0, 1] inputs.
questions.explanation: Self-assessment. If any step is unclear, trace the shapes with the shape-flow visualization and reread the preprocessing paragraph.

questions.question: What does `model.evaluate(test_images, test_labels)` return in Listing 2.7?
options: The predicted class for every test image
The test loss and the test accuracy
Only the test accuracy
The updated weights after training on the test set
questions.answer: The test loss and the test accuracy
questions.explanation: The listing unpacks the result into `test_loss, test_acc`: the compiled loss and the `accuracy` metric averaged over the test set. Per-image predictions come from `predict()` (p.44); `evaluate()` never updates weights.

questions.question: Training accuracy is 98.9 % and test accuracy 97.85 %. Compute both error rates and explain the authors' phrase 'almost double the error rate'.
questions.answer: Training error 1.1 %, test error 2.15 %; 2.15 / 1.1 ≈ 1.95, so the test error is almost twice the training error.
questions.explanation: Error rate = 1 - accuracy. A 1.1-point accuracy gap corresponds to nearly doubling the fraction of mistakes, which is why the authors express the gap in error terms.

questions.question: Define overfitting as the page does, and explain why it can only be detected by evaluating on data outside the training set.
questions.answer: Overfitting is the tendency of models to perform worse on new data than on their training data. Training accuracy alone cannot reveal it because it measures performance on the very data the model adapted to; only a held-out set shows the drop.
questions.explanation: The page defines overfitting as 'the fact that machine learning models tend to perform worse on new data than on their training data' and discovers it precisely by comparing `fit()`'s training accuracy with `evaluate()`'s test accuracy.

questions.question: According to section 2.2, what is a tensor?
options: A container for numerical data generalizing matrices to any number of axes
A synonym for a two-dimensional matrix
A Keras layer that stores weights
A TensorFlow-specific data type unavailable in NumPy
questions.answer: A container for numerical data generalizing matrices to any number of axes
questions.explanation: The page says a tensor is 'a container for data—usually numerical data' and that 'tensors are a generalization of matrices to an arbitrary number of dimensions'. Matrices are only the rank-2 case; layers are built *from* tensor operations; NumPy arrays are tensors too.

questions.question: Why do the authors prefer the word 'axis' to 'dimension' when talking about tensors?
questions.answer: Because 'dimension' is ambiguous in tensor context: it can mean the number of axes or the number of entries along an axis; 'axis' unambiguously means an index direction of the tensor.
questions.explanation: The page notes that 'in the context of tensors, a dimension is often called an axis'; p.46 spells out the 5D-vector vs 5D-tensor confusion that motivates this.

questions.question: Name the three topics the authors say the rest of this chapter and the next will explain, and what each corresponds to in the example.
questions.answer: Tensors (the data-storing objects going into the model), tensor operations (which layers are made of), and gradient descent (which lets the model learn from its training examples).
questions.explanation: This is the road map in the closing paragraph of section 2.1; sections 2.2, 2.3 and 2.4 cover them in that order.

questions.question: Can you explain, without notes, why 9,785 correct test digits out of 10,000 is a more trustworthy number than the 98.9 % printed during training?
questions.answer: The test digits were never used to adjust the weights, so their accuracy estimates performance on genuinely new data; the training accuracy is inflated by overfitting.
questions.explanation: Self-assessment on the central lesson of the page. If unsure, reread the overfitting paragraph and the analogy in the Deeper section.

questions.question: What does `x.ndim` return for `x = np.array([12, 3, 6, 14, 7])`?
questions.explanation: `ndim` is the number of axes (the rank). A vector has exactly one axis, so `ndim` is 1. Five is the number of entries, and `(5,)` is the shape (p.47), not `ndim`.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a '5D vector' and a '5D tensor' as the page describes it.
questions.answer: A 5D vector has one axis with five entries along it (rank 1); a 5D tensor has five axes, each with any number of entries (rank 5).
questions.explanation: The page states exactly this and notes that 'dimensionality' is ambiguous; 'tensor of rank 5' is the unambiguous phrase for five axes.

questions.question: Which statement about `x = np.array(12)` is correct?
options: It is a vector with one entry
It is a scalar tensor with `ndim == 0`
It is a matrix with one row and one column
It cannot be created; NumPy arrays need a list
questions.answer: It is a scalar tensor with `ndim == 0`
questions.explanation: The page shows `np.array(12)` displaying as `array(12)` with `ndim` 0: a rank-0 tensor. A one-entry vector would be `np.array([12])` (`ndim` 1); a 1 x 1 matrix would need two levels of brackets.

questions.question: The page says a matrix is 'an array of vectors'. How does this phrasing anticipate the way higher-rank tensors are built?
questions.answer: Each rank is defined by packing tensors of the previous rank into a new array: numbers into a vector, vectors into a matrix, and (p.47) matrices into a rank-3 tensor, and so on; every packing adds one axis.
questions.explanation: The definitions on the page are recursive, and p.47 continues: 'If you pack such matrices in a new array, you obtain a rank-3 tensor'.

questions.question: For the page's matrix `x`, what are `x[0]`, `x[1][3]`, and the number of axes and entries?
questions.answer: `x[0]` is `[5, 78, 2, 34, 0]` (first row); `x[1][3]` is 35; the matrix has 2 axes and 3 x 5 = 15 entries.
questions.explanation: Rows are indexed along the first axis and columns along the second (p.47 names `[5, 78, 2, 34, 0]` as the first row). Rank is 2 regardless of the 15 entries.

questions.question: Without looking, write a NumPy snippet creating a scalar, a vector and a matrix, and predict `ndim` for each. Then explain in one sentence why a 784-dimensional MNIST input vector has rank 1.
questions.answer: `np.array(12)` -> 0; `np.array([12, 3, 6, 14, 7])` -> 1; `np.array([[...], [...], [...]])` -> 2. The 784-dimensional input has 784 entries along a single axis, so one index suffices and its rank is 1.
questions.explanation: Self-check on the page's three examples and on the entries-vs-axes distinction.

questions.question: What is the shape of the rank-3 tensor built on this page by packing three 3 x 5 matrices?
questions.explanation: The new packing axis comes first (3 matrices), then the rows (3), then the columns (5), as the Shape bullet states. (9, 5) would be a rank-2 tensor obtained by stacking the rows, not packing the matrices.

questions.question: Name the three key attributes that define a tensor and the NumPy attribute that exposes each.
questions.answer: Number of axes (rank), `ndim`; shape, `shape`; data type, `dtype`.
questions.explanation: The page lists exactly these three; `ndim` is named on the page and `shape`/`dtype` are read off `train_images` on p.48.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly gives the shapes of a scalar and of a 5-entry vector?
questions.explanation: The page states that 'a vector has a shape with a single element, such as (5,), whereas a scalar has an empty shape, ()'. `(5)` is not a tuple in Python, and the other options describe rank-1 or rank-2 tensors of different sizes.

questions.question: In the matrix of p.46, why is `[5, 6, 7]` the first column? Give the index expression that selects it and the one that selects the first row.
questions.answer: The first column consists of the entries at position 0 of every row: 5, 6, 7. It is `x[:, 0]`; the first row is `x[0]` (or `x[0, :]`), equal to `[5, 78, 2, 34, 0]`.
questions.explanation: Rows are entries along axis 0 and columns entries along axis 1; fixing the column index to 0 and taking all rows gives the first column.

questions.question: Explain how the first MNIST example on p.44 changed each of the three key attributes of `train_images`.
questions.answer: `reshape((60000, 28 * 28))` changed the rank from 3 to 2 and the shape from (60000, 28, 28) to (60000, 784); `astype("float32")` changed the dtype from uint8 to float32; dividing by 255 changed the values but none of the three attributes.
questions.explanation: The attributes defined on this page are exactly what the preprocessing of Listing 2.4 manipulated; p.48 confirms the original rank, shape and dtype.

questions.question: Up to what rank do tensors typically go in deep learning, and what kind of data needs the highest rank?
questions.answer: Ranks 0 to 4 are typical; video data needs rank 5.
questions.explanation: Stated directly on the page; p.50 and p.52 show video as (samples, frames, height, width, channels).

questions.question: Given any NumPy array, can you state its rank, shape, dtype and number of elements without running code, just from how it is written? Try it on the page's rank-3 example.
questions.answer: Rank 3 (three bracket levels), shape (3, 3, 5), dtype integer (int64 by default on most platforms), 45 elements.
questions.explanation: Self-assessment on reading the three attributes directly from a literal; the dtype of integer literals is NumPy's platform default integer, a detail not in the book.

questions.question: What does `train_images.shape == (60000, 28, 28)` with `dtype == uint8` tell you?
options: 60,000 colour images of 28 x 28 pixels with 3 channels
60,000 grayscale images of 28 x 28 pixels with integer values 0-255
28 images of 60000 x 28 pixels
60,000 flattened vectors of 784 floating-point values
questions.answer: 60,000 grayscale images of 28 x 28 pixels with integer values 0-255
questions.explanation: The page interprets the attributes as 'an array of 60,000 matrices of 28 x 28 integers', each a grayscale image with coefficients 0-255. There is no channel axis (no colour), the first axis is the samples axis, and the flattened float32 form only exists after Listing 2.4 on p.44.

questions.question: What is the shape and rank of `digit = train_images[4]`, and why?
questions.answer: Shape (28, 28), rank 2: indexing the first axis of the rank-3 tensor removes that axis, leaving one image matrix.
questions.explanation: The page describes the tensor as an array of 60,000 matrices; selecting one entry along the first axis returns one of those matrices. `imshow` requires a 2-D array, which is why this works.

questions.question: Why does the page cast the image data to float32 on p.44 but leave `train_labels` as integers?
options: Labels are never used during training
The loss `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` consumes integer class labels directly, while the network's arithmetic runs in float32
uint8 labels are automatically converted to images
Matplotlib requires integer labels
questions.answer: The loss `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` consumes integer class labels directly, while the network's arithmetic runs in float32
questions.explanation: `train_labels[4]` is simply the integer 9, and p.44 chose a 'sparse' loss precisely so integer labels can be used. The pixel data is cast so that the network's float32 computations and the [0, 1] rescaling work correctly.

questions.question: How many pixel values does `train_images` hold, and roughly how much memory does it take as uint8?
questions.answer: 60000 x 28 x 28 = 47,040,000 values; at 1 byte each, about 47 MB.
questions.explanation: The element count is the product of the shape entries; uint8 uses one byte per value. (Memory figures are not stated on this page; the same reasoning appears on p.52 for a video tensor.)

questions.question: Explain what `cmap=plt.cm.binary` does in Listing 2.8 and why the digit in Figure 2.2 appears dark on a light background.
questions.answer: The colour map decides how intensities 0-255 are turned into colours; `binary` maps 0 to white and 255 to black, so the high-valued pen strokes show up dark.
questions.explanation: `imshow` has no intrinsic notion of 'ink'; the colour map determines the rendering, and the book chooses `binary` to get a natural pen-on-paper look.

questions.question: Why is it guaranteed that `train_labels[4]` describes the image `train_images[4]`?
questions.answer: Because the image and label arrays were loaded together with a one-to-one correspondence by position (p.42); both have 60,000 entries along their first axis indexed identically.
questions.explanation: The page says 'naturally, the corresponding label is just the integer 9', relying on the alignment stated when the data was introduced.

questions.question: Without running code, write down the `ndim`, `shape` and `dtype` you expect for `test_images` and `test_labels`, then explain how you would display the first test digit.
questions.answer: `test_images`: ndim 3, shape (10000, 28, 28), uint8; `test_labels`: ndim 1, shape (10000,), uint8. Display with `plt.imshow(test_images[0], cmap=plt.cm.binary); plt.show()`.
questions.explanation: Self-assessment transferring the page's routine to the test arrays (their sizes come from p.44, where 10000 is used in the reshape).

questions.question: What is the shape of `train_images[10:100]` when `train_images` has shape `(60000, 28, 28)`?
questions.explanation: The range 10:100 is half-open, so it contains 100 − 10 = 90 indices; the other two axes are untouched. (91, 28, 28) wrongly includes index 100; (90, 784) would require a reshape, which slicing does not do; (28, 28) is what a single integer index such as `train_images[4]` returns.

questions.question: Rewrite `train_images[:, 7:-7, 7:-7]` without negative indices, and give the resulting shape.
questions.explanation: On an axis of length 28, `-7` translates to 28 − 7 = 21. Rows and columns 7..20 are kept, 14 of each, for all 60,000 images.

questions.question: Why are `train_images[10:100]`, `train_images[10:100, :, :]` and `train_images[10:100, 0:28, 0:28]` all equivalent?
questions.answer: Because an index expression has one range per axis; omitted trailing axes and `:` both mean "the entire axis", and `0:28` is the explicit form of the whole axis when its length is 28. All three therefore restrict only axis 0 to 10..99.
questions.explanation: The page states that `:` is equivalent to selecting the entire axis and that the detailed notation specifies a start and stop index along each axis; the page's callouts mark both longer forms as equivalent to the first.

questions.question: Which slice selects the bottom-right 14 × 14 pixels of every MNIST image?
options: train_images[14:, 14:]
train_images[:, :14, :14]
train_images[:, 14:, 14:]
train_images[:, 14:, :14]
questions.answer: train_images[:, 14:, 14:]
questions.explanation: Axis 0 must stay `:` to keep all images; rows 14..27 are the bottom half and columns 14..27 the right half. `train_images[14:, 14:]` would slice the samples axis and the row axis instead; `[:, :14, :14]` is the top-left quadrant; `[:, 14:, :14]` is bottom-left.

questions.question: In deep learning data tensors, which axis is the samples axis, and what is a "sample" in the MNIST example?
questions.answer: Axis 0 (the first axis); in MNIST a sample is one digit image.
questions.explanation: The page states that the first axis, axis 0 because indexing starts at 0, is the samples axis in all data tensors you will come across, and that for MNIST the samples are images of digits.

questions.question: How does the notion of a data batch relate to tensor slicing?
questions.answer: A batch is a fixed-size group of samples, which is exactly a slice along the samples axis: with batch size 128, the first batch is `train_images[:128]`, the next `train_images[128:256]`, and in general `train_images[128 * n:128 * (n + 1)]` (p.50).
questions.explanation: Because axis 0 indexes samples, taking consecutive half-open ranges of length 128 along it partitions the dataset into non-overlapping batches of identical shape `(128, 28, 28)`.

questions.question: Without running code, can you write the slice that keeps the top-left 7 × 7 corner of images #0..#999 and state its shape?
questions.explanation: Range of length 1000 on the samples axis, rows 0..6 and columns 0..6 (top and left, since index 0 is the top-left). If you got this, you have the per-axis slicing rule down; if not, re-read the equivalence examples and the two crop examples on the page.

questions.question: With a batch size of 128, which image indices does `train_images[128 * n : 128 * (n + 1)]` select when n = 3?
questions.answer: Indices 384 through 511 (the slice `[384:512]`), 128 images.
questions.explanation: 128 × 3 = 384 is the inclusive start and 128 × 4 = 512 the exclusive stop, so the batch holds images 384..511.

questions.question: What does the book call axis 0 of a batch tensor?
options: The features axis
The batch axis (or batch dimension)
The channels axis
The time axis
questions.answer: The batch axis (or batch dimension)
questions.explanation: The page states that for a batch tensor the first axis is called the batch axis or batch dimension. The features axis is axis 1 of vector data; the channels axis is the last axis of image data; the time axis is axis 1 of sequence data (p.51).

questions.question: Which shape template does the book give for image data?
options: (samples, channels, height, width)
(samples, height, width)
(samples, height, width, channels)
(height, width, channels)
questions.answer: (samples, height, width, channels)
questions.explanation: Images are rank-4 tensors `(samples, height, width, channels)` on this page (channels-last). `(samples, channels, height, width)` is the channels-first convention mentioned on p.51 for PyTorch, not the template given here; `(samples, height, width)` lacks the channels axis that image tensors keep even for grayscale; `(height, width, channels)` is one image, not a dataset.

questions.question: A dataset records age, gender and income for 100,000 people. What is its tensor shape and rank, and what does each axis mean?
questions.answer: Shape `(100000, 3)`, rank 2; axis 0 is the samples axis (people) and axis 1 is the features axis (age, gender, income).
questions.explanation: Each person is a vector of three values; stacking 100,000 such vectors gives a rank-2 tensor, exactly the actuarial example on the page.

questions.question: Why does the rank of the dataset tensor increase by one from vector data to timeseries to images to video?
questions.answer: Because each category adds one level of structure to a single sample (a vector → a sequence of vectors → a grid of channel vectors → a sequence of grids), and the dataset always prepends one samples axis. Rank = 1 + rank of one sample: 2, 3, 4, 5.
questions.explanation: The page's four bullets describe each sample's structure explicitly: a vector, a sequence of length `timesteps` of feature vectors, a 2D grid of pixels each a vector of channels, and a sequence of `frames` images. Each description nests the previous one inside one more axis.

questions.question: MNIST has 60,000 training images. With batch size 128, how many batches are there, and how many images are in the last one?
questions.answer: 469 batches; the last (n = 468) contains 60000 − 468 × 128 = 96 images.
questions.explanation: 60000 / 128 = 468.75, so 468 full batches cover 59,904 images and a 469th partial batch holds the remaining 96. The slice `train_images[59904:60032]` is clipped by NumPy to the available 96 rows. (This computation extends the page's formula; the numbers are not in the book.)

questions.question: Can you name, from memory, the four data categories on this page with their rank and shape template?
questions.answer: Vector data, rank 2, `(samples, features)`; timeseries/sequence data, rank 3, `(samples, timesteps, features)`; images, rank 4, `(samples, height, width, channels)`; video, rank 5, `(samples, frames, height, width, channels)`.
questions.explanation: These four templates are reused throughout the book; if any is missing, re-read the bullet list and note that every one starts with `samples`.

questions.question: In the stock-price example, what does the shape `(250, 390, 3)` represent?
options: 250 minutes, 390 stocks, 3 days
250 trading days, 390 minutes per day, 3 values per minute
250 stocks, 390 days, 3 prices
250 features, 390 timesteps, 3 samples
questions.answer: 250 trading days, 390 minutes per day, 3 values per minute
questions.explanation: Axis 0 is samples (each sample is one day), axis 1 is the time axis (390 minutes), axis 2 is features (current price, past-minute high, past-minute low). The other options either reorder the axes (features/timesteps/samples is the reverse order) or invent quantities (stocks) the example does not contain.

questions.question: Which axis is the time axis in a sequence data tensor, and why that one?
questions.answer: Axis 1 (the second axis), by convention: axis 0 is reserved for samples, so time is the first axis inside each sample, followed by features.
questions.explanation: The page states the convention explicitly; it combines with the samples-axis convention of p.49 to fix the layout `(samples, timesteps, features)`.

questions.question: A tweet is 280 characters from an alphabet of 128 symbols, one-hot encoded. What is the shape of one tweet, and of a dataset of 1 million tweets? How many 1s does the dataset tensor contain?
questions.answer: One tweet: `(280, 128)`; the dataset: `(1000000, 280, 128)`; it contains 1,000,000 × 280 = 280,000,000 ones (exactly one per character).
questions.explanation: Each character is a length-128 binary vector with a single 1, so a tweet stacks 280 of them into a `(280, 128)` matrix and the dataset stacks a million matrices. The count of ones is one per character position; the total number of entries, 3.584 × 10^10, is mostly zeros. (The count of ones is a derived number, not stated in the book.)

questions.question: According to the book, how should a batch of 128 grayscale 256 × 256 images be stored in the channels-last convention?
questions.explanation: Image tensors keep a channels axis even for grayscale, and channels-last puts it at the end. `(128, 256, 256)` drops the channel axis; `(128, 1, 256, 256)` is the channels-first layout (p.52); `(256, 256, 128)` has no samples axis in front.

questions.question: Why does the book store grayscale images with a channels axis of size 1 instead of as rank-2 matrices?
questions.answer: By convention image tensors are always rank 3 per image (`height, width, channels`), so that grayscale and color images share one format; the channel axis simply has size 1 for grayscale.
questions.explanation: The page says grayscale images *could* be rank 2 but that by convention image tensors are always rank 3 with a one-dimensional color channel. A uniform format lets the same layers (e.g. `Conv2D`) process both kinds of image.

questions.question: Name the two image-layout conventions, give their shape templates, and say which frameworks use each.
questions.answer: Channels-last `(samples, height, width, color_depth)`, standard in JAX, TensorFlow and most other tools; channels-first `(samples, color_depth, height, width)`, standard in PyTorch.
questions.explanation: Both appear verbatim on the page; the next page adds that Keras supports both formats.

questions.question: Given a dataset description, can you say what one sample is, write its shape, and then write the dataset shape? Test yourself: hourly temperature and humidity readings for 30 days from each of 50 weather stations, one sample per station-day.
questions.answer: One sample = one station-day = 24 hourly readings of 2 features → `(24, 2)`; the dataset = 50 × 30 = 1500 samples → `(1500, 24, 2)`, with time on axis 1.
questions.explanation: This follows the stock-price pattern: per-step vector `(2,)`, per-sample matrix `(24, 2)`, dataset `(1500, 24, 2)`. If you placed time on axis 0 or 2, revisit the convention stated on this page.

questions.question: Verify the book's count: how many values are in a tensor of shape `(4, 240, 144, 256, 3)`, and how many bytes does it occupy as float32?
questions.explanation: The element count is the product of all axis lengths, and float32 stores each value in 32 bits = 4 bytes, matching the 425 MB stated on the page.

questions.question: In the channels-first convention, how is the batch of 128 color 256 × 256 images stored?
questions.explanation: Channels-first puts color depth right after the batch axis. `(128, 256, 256, 3)` is channels-last; `(3, 128, 256, 256)` puts channels before samples, which no convention does; `(128, 256, 3, 256)` places channels between height and width.

questions.question: Why are real-world video files much lighter than the 425 MB tensor computed on the page?
questions.answer: Because they are not stored as float32 values and they are compressed by a large factor (for example with MPEG).
questions.explanation: The page gives both reasons: dtype (float32 uses 4 bytes per value, far more than needed for pixel data) and compression (codecs such as MPEG shrink the data substantially).

questions.question: What analogy do the authors use to introduce tensor operations, and what claim does it support?
questions.answer: Just as any computer program reduces to a small set of binary operations on binary inputs (AND, OR, NOR, …), all transformations learned by deep neural networks reduce to a handful of tensor operations (adding, multiplying tensors, and so on) applied to numeric tensors.
questions.explanation: The analogy frames section 2.3: a deep network, however complex, is composed from a few simple primitives, which the section then catalogues.

questions.question: In `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)`, what are `W` and `b`?
options: Two extra input tensors supplied with each batch
A matrix and a vector that are attributes of the Dense layer
Hyperparameters chosen by the user, like the number of units
The output shape and the batch size
questions.answer: A matrix and a vector that are attributes of the Dense layer
questions.explanation: The page says `W` is a matrix and `b` a vector, both attributes of the layer. They are not inputs (only `input` is passed in), not hyperparameters (they are learned, whereas 512 units is a hyperparameter), and not shapes.

questions.question: If `input` has shape `(128, 784)` and the layer is `Dense(512, activation="relu")`, what are the shapes of `W`, `b` and `output`?
questions.explanation: `matmul(input, W)` requires W's first axis to match the 784 input features and its second axis to be the 512 units; `b` has one entry per unit and is added to every row; the output keeps the 128 samples and has 512 features. (Shapes are derived from the formula; the page states the formula but not these specific numbers.)

questions.question: Can you list the three tensor operations hidden in `relu(matmul(input, W) + b)`, in the order they are executed, and say which upcoming subsection explains each?
questions.answer: 1. Tensor product `matmul(input, W)` (2.3.3, p.56); 2. addition of the vector `b` to the matrix, which relies on broadcasting (2.3.1 element-wise ops p.53 and 2.3.2 broadcasting p.54); 3. element-wise `relu` (2.3.1, p.53).
questions.explanation: The next page lists exactly these three operations; the chapter outline shows where each is treated. If you could not name them, re-read the last paragraph of this page and p.53.

questions.question: What does "relu" stand for, and what does relu(x) compute?
questions.answer: REctified Linear Unit; relu(x) = max(x, 0), so negatives become 0 and non-negatives pass unchanged.
questions.explanation: Both the expansion of the acronym and the definition `max(x, 0)` are given in the third bullet on the page.

questions.question: Which of the three operations in `relu(matmul(input, W) + b)` is NOT element-wise?
options: The relu
The addition of b
The tensor product matmul
All three are element-wise
questions.answer: The tensor product matmul
questions.explanation: The page states that relu and addition are element-wise. The tensor product is treated separately (p.56) because each output entry combines a whole row of the input with a whole column of W; it is not an independent per-entry operation.

questions.question: Why are element-wise operations "highly amenable to massively parallel implementations"?
questions.answer: Because each output entry depends only on the corresponding input entry (or entries), so all entries can be computed independently and simultaneously, in any order, with no communication between them.
questions.explanation: The page defines element-wise operations as applied independently to each entry; independence is exactly the condition under which work can be distributed across many parallel units (vectorized implementations, SIMD, GPU threads).

questions.question: What is the purpose of the line `x = x.copy()` in `naive_relu` and `naive_add`?
options: To convert x to float32
To avoid overwriting the input tensor
To make the loops run faster
To check that x is rank 2
questions.answer: To avoid overwriting the input tensor
questions.explanation: The margin callout says exactly this: the functions assign into `x[i, j]`, so without a copy they would mutate the caller's array. Copying does not change dtype, does not speed up the loops, and the rank check is done by the separate `assert len(x.shape) == 2`.

questions.question: Compute `naive_relu(x)` and `naive_add(x, y)` for x = [[-2, 3], [0, -1]] and y = [[1, 1], [2, 2]].
questions.explanation: relu replaces each negative entry with 0 and keeps 3 and 0. Addition pairs entries position by position: −2+1, 3+1, 0+2, −1+2.

questions.question: Why would `naive_add` fail on the Dense layer's `matmul(input, W) + b`, and which upcoming idea fixes this?
questions.answer: Because `naive_add` asserts `x.shape == y.shape`, while the Dense layer adds a rank-2 matrix to a rank-1 vector `b`; broadcasting (2.3.2, p.54) virtually expands the vector to the matrix shape so the element-wise addition can proceed.
questions.explanation: The page's second bullet says the addition is between the resulting matrix and a vector, and `naive_add` requires identical rank-2 shapes; p.54 opens by pointing out this limitation and introducing broadcasting.

questions.question: What does NumPy do instead of running Python loops for element-wise operations, according to the page?
questions.answer: It provides well-optimized built-in functions that delegate the heavy lifting to a BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms) implementation, low-level routines written in Fortran or C.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states this; p.54 completes the sentence and demonstrates the speed difference (0.02 s vs 2.45 s).

questions.question: Can you write, from memory, a `naive_subtract(x, y)` on the same pattern as `naive_add`, and say which single line you would change?
questions.answer: Identical to `naive_add` except the inner line becomes `x[i, j] -= y[i, j]`.
questions.explanation: The page says element-wise multiplication, subtraction and so on follow the same principle; the loop structure, assertions and copy are unchanged. If you were unsure, re-read `naive_add` and note that only the per-entry operation defines which element-wise function it is.

questions.question: Which NumPy expression implements the element-wise relu used on this page?
options: np.max(z, 0.0)
np.maximum(z, 0.0)
z.max(axis=0)
questions.answer: np.maximum(z, 0.0)
questions.explanation: `np.maximum` takes the element-wise maximum of z and 0.0. `np.max(z, 0.0)` and `z.max(axis=0)` are reductions along an axis; `np.clip(z, 0.0, 0.0)` would set every value to 0.

questions.question: Using the book's timings, how many times faster is the vectorized version than the naive version? And roughly how much time per iteration does each take?
questions.answer: About 2.45 / 0.02 ≈ 122×. Per iteration: 0.02 s / 1000 = 20 µs for the vectorized version, 2.45 s / 1000 = 2.45 ms for the naive one.
questions.explanation: Both loops run 1,000 iterations, so dividing the total time by 1,000 gives the per-iteration cost; the ratio of totals gives the speed-up.

questions.question: Why are element-wise operations particularly well suited to GPUs?
questions.answer: Because each output entry depends only on the corresponding input entries, all entries can be computed independently and simultaneously by the GPU's many parallel cores via vectorized CUDA kernels.
questions.explanation: The page says element-wise ops on GPU run via fully vectorized CUDA implementations that best use the highly parallel chip; p.53 explains that element-wise ops are highly amenable to massive parallelism.

questions.question: What limitation of naive_add motivates section 2.3.2?
questions.answer: It only supports adding rank-2 tensors with identical shapes, whereas the Dense layer adds a rank-2 tensor and a vector.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph of 2.3.2 states this directly.

questions.question: A tensor of shape (10,) is added to one of shape (32, 10). After the first broadcasting step described on this page, what is the smaller tensor's shape?
questions.explanation: Step 1 adds a broadcast axis so the ndim becomes 2, giving (1, 10) (confirmed on p.55). (10, 1) would put the axis in the wrong place; (32, 10) is the result only after step 2 (repetition).

questions.question: What does the phrase 'when possible, and if there's no ambiguity' imply about broadcasting?
questions.answer: Broadcasting does not apply to every pair of shapes; the smaller tensor's shape must be compatible with (align to the trailing axes of) the larger tensor's shape, otherwise the operation fails.
questions.explanation: p.55 states the general condition: shapes (a, b, … n, n+1, … m) and (n, n+1, … m) broadcast over axes a through n−1. Beyond the book, NumPy also allows axes of size 1 to stretch.

questions.question: Run both timing snippets on your own machine. Do you get a similar ratio? What happens to the ratio if you make the arrays (200, 1000)?
questions.answer: Answers vary by hardware; typically the ratio stays large and often grows with larger arrays, because the fixed per-call overhead of NumPy becomes negligible while the Python loop cost scales linearly with the number of elements.
questions.explanation: This checks that you understand the source of the speed-up: per-element interpreter overhead versus per-call overhead.

questions.question: After `y = np.expand_dims(y, axis=0)` on a vector `y` of shape (10,), what is `y.shape`?
questions.explanation: `axis=0` inserts a new leading axis of size 1, giving (1, 10) as the page states. (10, 1) would require axis=1; (10,) is the original shape; (32, 10) is only reached after tiling.

questions.question: What does the tuple `(32, 1)` mean in `Y = np.tile(y, (32, 1))`?
questions.answer: Repeat y 32 times along axis 0 and once along axis 1, producing Y of shape (32, 10) with every row equal to y.
questions.explanation: np.tile takes a per-axis repetition count; 32 copies stacked along the first axis and no extra copies along the second yield (32, 10), and Y[i, :] == y for all i.

questions.question: The page says the repetition in broadcasting is 'entirely virtual'. What does that mean and why does it matter?
questions.answer: No new rank-2 tensor holding 32 copies of y is allocated; the operation simply reuses y[j] for every row i. This avoids wasting memory and time, which would be 'terribly inefficient' for large batches.
questions.explanation: The authors contrast the algorithmic level (where y is conceptually repeated) with the memory level (where it is not). The naive loop demonstrates the algorithm: indexing y[j] inside the row loop achieves the repetition without storage.

questions.question: According to the general rule on this page, which pair of shapes is compatible for a broadcast element-wise operation?
questions.explanation: The smaller shape must equal the trailing axes of the larger: (3,) matches the last axis of (64, 28, 28, 3), so broadcasting happens over the first three axes. (32,) does not match the trailing 10 of (32, 10); (10, 32) is a prefix, not a suffix, of (10, 32, 3); (5, 4) and (4, 5) have the same rank but mismatched trailing axes.

questions.question: Let X = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] and y = [10, 20, 30]. Compute X + y using the broadcasting rule Z_ij = X_ij + y_j.
questions.explanation: Each row of X receives the same vector y: row 0 becomes (1+10, 2+20, 3+30) and row 1 becomes (4+10, 5+20, 6+30). The index into y depends only on the column j.

questions.question: Why does `naive_add_matrix_and_vector` call `x = x.copy()` before the loops?
questions.answer: To avoid overwriting the input tensor; the function modifies x in place inside the loops, so without the copy the caller's array would be mutated.
questions.explanation: The printed callout says 'Avoids overwriting the input tensor'. The in-place `x[i, j] += y[j]` would otherwise change the array passed in.

questions.question: Without looking, write down the two steps of broadcasting and give the shapes y passes through in the (32, 10) + (10,) example. Then explain in one sentence why NumPy does not actually perform step 2 in memory.
questions.answer: Step 1: add broadcast axes to match ndim — (10,) → (1, 10). Step 2: repeat along the new axes — (1, 10) → (32, 10). NumPy skips the physical copy because the same y[j] can be read for every row, making a materialised copy wasteful.
questions.explanation: Check your answer against the bullets and the three code snippets on the page; the key insight is that the repetition is algorithmic, not a memory allocation.

questions.question: x has shape (64, 3, 32, 10) and y has shape (32, 10). What is the shape of np.maximum(x, y)?
options: It raises a shape error
questions.explanation: y matches the trailing axes of x, so it is broadcast over the leading (64, 3) axes and the output takes x's shape, as the callout says. (32, 10) and (64, 3) are partial shapes; no error occurs because the trailing axes agree.

questions.question: Give the three ways shown on this page to compute a tensor product in code.
questions.answer: np.matmul(x, y) in NumPy, keras.ops.matmul(x, y) in Keras, and the shorthand x @ y.
questions.explanation: The page names np.matmul and keras.ops.matmul and shows that z = x @ y is equivalent to z = np.matmul(x, y).

questions.question: Using naive_vector_product, compute the product of x = [1, 2, 3] and y = [4, 5, 6].
questions.explanation: z = 1·4 + 2·5 + 3·6 = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32. The loop accumulates each x[i]*y[i] into z starting from 0.0.

questions.question: Which statement about the product of two vectors is correct according to the page?
options: It returns a vector of the same length as the inputs
It returns a scalar and requires both vectors to have the same number of elements
It returns a matrix of shape (n, n)
It works for vectors of any two lengths
questions.answer: It returns a scalar and requires both vectors to have the same number of elements
questions.explanation: The closing paragraph states both facts. A same-length vector would be the element-wise product x * y; an (n, n) matrix would be an outer product, not discussed here; different lengths fail the assert x.shape[0] == y.shape[0].

questions.question: Why does the page call the operation 'dot product'?
questions.answer: Because in mathematical notation it is written with a dot: z = x • y.
questions.explanation: The page says 'you'd note the operation with a dot (•) (hence the name "dot product")'. The code names matmul and tensor product refer to the same operation.

questions.question: Contrast how np.maximum and the vector product treat the shapes of their inputs.
questions.answer: np.maximum is element-wise: the output keeps the (larger) input shape and broadcasting fills in missing axes. The vector product contracts the shared axis: two (32,) vectors become a single scalar.
questions.explanation: Element-wise operations never change rank, while the tensor product sums over an axis and removes it — the key difference between the two halves of this page.

questions.question: Without looking, write naive_vector_product from memory, including its three asserts. Then explain which assert encodes the 'same number of elements' rule.
questions.answer: Two rank-1 asserts (len(x.shape) == 1, len(y.shape) == 1), then assert x.shape[0] == y.shape[0] — this third one is the same-length rule; z = 0.0; loop over i accumulating x[i] * y[i]; return z.
questions.explanation: Compare with the listing on the page. The third assert is the compatibility condition the closing paragraph refers to.

questions.question: x has shape (4, 3) and y has shape (3, 5). What is the shape of matmul(x, y)?
options: Undefined — shapes are incompatible
questions.explanation: x.shape[1] == y.shape[0] (3 == 3) so the product is defined, and the result has shape (x.shape[0], y.shape[1]) = (4, 5). (3, 3) would be the contracted axis; (5, 4) is the shape of y^T x^T, not of x @ y.

questions.question: Compute naive_matrix_vector_product(x, y) for x = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and y = [1, 1]. Then compute matmul(y, x) and comment.
questions.answer: x @ y = [3, 7]; y @ x = [4, 6]. The results differ, showing matmul is not symmetric.
questions.explanation: z[0] = 1·1 + 2·1 = 3, z[1] = 3·1 + 4·1 = 7. For y @ x the entries are 1·1 + 1·3 = 4 and 1·2 + 1·4 = 6. As the page notes, once an operand has ndim > 1 the order matters.

questions.question: In naive_matrix_product, what do row_x = x[i, :] and column_y = y[:, j] represent, and why must they have the same length?
questions.answer: Row i of x and column j of y; z[i, j] is their vector product, which is only defined for equal lengths — hence x.shape[1] == y.shape[0].
questions.explanation: The text says the coefficients are the vector products between the rows of x and the columns of y; the p.56 vector product requires x.shape[0] == y.shape[0] for its two inputs.

questions.question: The second implementation of naive_matrix_vector_product calls naive_vector_product. What relationship does this reveal?
questions.answer: A matrix–vector product is just a vector product repeated for each row of the matrix: z[i] is the dot product of row i with y.
questions.explanation: The page says the rewrite 'highlights the relationship between a matrix-vector product and a vector product'. The inner j loop of the first version is exactly the body of naive_vector_product.

questions.question: Which pair of shapes can NOT be multiplied with matmul(x, y)?
questions.explanation: The rule is x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]. For (3, 2) and (3, 2), 2 ≠ 3, so the product is undefined — same shape is not the criterion. The other pairs satisfy 3 == 3, 5 == 5 and 4 == 4.

questions.question: What does the line z = np.zeros((x.shape[0], y.shape[1])) tell you about the output of a matrix product?
questions.answer: The result has one row per row of x and one column per column of y — shape (x.shape[0], y.shape[1]) — and is filled in entry by entry starting from zeros.
questions.explanation: The callout says it 'returns a matrix of 0s with a specific shape'; that shape is the output shape rule stated in the text.

questions.question: Without looking, write the three asserts of naive_matrix_product and the shape of z. Then explain in one sentence why matmul(input, W) in a Dense layer with input (32, 784) requires W to have 784 rows.
questions.answer: len(x.shape) == 2, len(y.shape) == 2, x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]; z has shape (x.shape[0], y.shape[1]). W needs 784 rows because the compatibility rule requires input.shape[1] (784) to equal W.shape[0].
questions.explanation: Compare with the listing; the Dense-layer application follows directly from the compatibility rule stated on this page.

questions.question: In figure 2.5, x has shape (a, b) and y has shape (b, c). Which statement is correct?
options: The height of x must equal the height of y
The width of x must equal the height of y, and z has shape (a, c)
The width of x must equal the width of y, and z has shape (b, b)
z has shape (c, a)
questions.answer: The width of x must equal the height of y, and z has shape (a, c)
questions.explanation: The text says 'the width of x must match the height of y' (both are b), and the figure labels z.shape as (a, c). Heights (a vs b) and widths (b vs c) need not match, and (c, a) reverses the output axes.

questions.question: Using the rules on this page, what is the shape of (a, b, c, d) • (d, e)? And of (32, 10, 64) • (64,)?
questions.answer: (a, b, c, e); and (32, 10) for the second case.
questions.explanation: The shared axis d (or 64) is contracted; the leading axes remain and the right operand's remaining axis e (if any) is appended. For a vector right operand nothing is appended.

questions.question: Let x = [[1, 0, 2], [0, 1, 1]] (shape (2, 3)) and y = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]] (shape (3, 2)). Compute z = x • y following naive_matrix_product.
questions.explanation: z[0,0] = 1·1 + 0·3 + 2·5 = 11; z[0,1] = 1·2 + 0·4 + 2·6 = 14; z[1,0] = 0·1 + 1·3 + 1·5 = 8; z[1,1] = 0·2 + 1·4 + 1·6 = 10. Each cell is the vector product of a row of x and a column of y; the shape is (a, c) = (2, 2).

questions.question: Why do the authors suggest you will often draw box diagrams like figure 2.5?
questions.answer: Because the diagram makes shape compatibility visible — matching edges show which axes must agree and what the output shape is — which is essential when developing new algorithms whose tensor shapes must line up.
questions.explanation: The text says 'If you go on to develop new machine learning algorithms, you'll likely be drawing such diagrams often'; the picture encodes the compatibility condition, output shape and per-cell computation at once.

questions.question: What does train_images.reshape((60000, 28 * 28)) produce?
options: A tensor of shape (60000, 28, 28) with normalised pixels
A tensor of shape (60000, 784) with the same pixel values rearranged
A tensor of shape (784, 60000)
A tensor with 28 * 28 = 784 images
questions.answer: A tensor of shape (60000, 784) with the same pixel values rearranged
questions.explanation: Reshaping to (60000, 28 * 28) flattens each 28 × 28 image into a 784-vector; values are unchanged and the sample count stays 60000. Normalisation is a separate step; (784, 60000) would be a transpose; 784 is the number of pixels, not images.

questions.question: Reshaping was not used inside the Dense layers of the first example. Where was it used instead?
questions.answer: In preprocessing: the digit images were reshaped from (60000, 28, 28) to (60000, 784) before being fed into the model.
questions.explanation: The text states it was used 'when we preprocessed the digits data before feeding it into our model', with the reshape line shown.

questions.question: Sketch figure 2.5 from memory for x of shape (3, 4) and y of shape (4, 2): label a, b, c, mark where z[2, 1] comes from, and state z's shape.
questions.answer: a = 3, b = 4, c = 2; z[2, 1] is the dot product of row 2 of x (length 4) with column 1 of y (length 4); z has shape (3, 2).
questions.explanation: Compare your sketch with the figure: x at the left (3 tall, 4 wide), y above z (4 tall, 2 wide), z at the corner (3 × 2).

questions.question: x = [[0., 1.], [2., 3.], [4., 5.]] has shape (3, 2). What does x.reshape((2, 3)) return?
options: An error, because the shapes differ
questions.explanation: The page's output shows the values refilled in their original order, three per row. [[0, 2, 4], [1, 3, 5]] is the transpose, not the reshape; the shapes (3, 2) and (2, 3) both hold 6 elements, so no error occurs.

questions.question: What invariant must every reshape satisfy, and why would reshape((4, 2)) fail for the 6-element matrix on this page?
questions.answer: The reshaped tensor must have the same total number of coefficients; 4 × 2 = 8 ≠ 6.
questions.explanation: The authors state that 'the reshaped tensor has the same total number of coefficients as the initial tensor'.

questions.question: Define transposition as the page does and give the shape of np.transpose(np.zeros((300, 20))).
questions.answer: Exchanging a matrix's rows and columns so that x[i, :] becomes x[:, i]; the result has shape (20, 300).
questions.explanation: The listing shows x.shape printing (20, 300) after np.transpose; the shape tuple is reversed.

questions.question: With A = [0.5, 1] and B = [1, 0.25], compute A + B and describe it geometrically.
questions.answer: A + B = [1.5, 1.25]; geometrically it is the point reached by placing arrow B at the head of arrow A — point A copied to a new location displaced by B.
questions.explanation: Add coordinates: 0.5 + 1 = 1.5 and 1 + 0.25 = 1.25. The page describes the sum as chaining the arrows (figure 2.8).

questions.question: Why do the authors claim that all tensor operations have a geometric interpretation?
questions.answer: Because the contents of tensors can be interpreted as coordinates of points in some geometric space, so any operation on those numbers is a transformation of points in that space.
questions.explanation: This is the opening sentence of 2.3.5. The claim sets up the view of a neural network as a chain of geometric transformations (p.62).

questions.question: Which statement about transposition and reshaping is correct?
options: Transposition is presented as a special case of reshaping
Transposition changes the number of coefficients
Reshaping always swaps rows and columns
np.transpose only works on square matrices
questions.answer: Transposition is presented as a special case of reshaping
questions.explanation: The page says 'A special case of reshaping that's commonly encountered is transposition'. Neither operation changes the element count; reshaping in general does not swap rows and columns (it refills in order); the example transposes a non-square (300, 20) matrix.

questions.question: Draw A = [0.5, 1] as a point and as an arrow, then draw B = [1, 0.25] chained from A's head. Mark the sum and check its coordinates. Can you explain why the pictures 'point' and 'arrow' describe the same vector?
questions.answer: The sum lands at (1.5, 1.25). A point gives the location; the arrow from the origin to that location carries the same two numbers as a displacement — both are the vector [0.5, 1].
questions.explanation: Compare with figures 2.6–2.8 on p.60; the arrow picture is what makes addition a geometric chaining operation.

questions.question: According to the page, what does tensor addition represent geometrically when applied to all points of an object?
options: Rotating the object about the origin
Scaling the object by a fixed factor
Translating the object — moving it without distortion
Reflecting the object across an axis
questions.answer: Translating the object — moving it without distortion
questions.explanation: The text says tensor addition 'represents the action of translating an object (moving the object without distorting it) by a certain amount in a certain direction'. Rotation and scaling are matrix products (p.61); reflection is not discussed here.

questions.question: What two properties of the move from A to A + B are determined by the vector B?
questions.answer: Its distance and its direction.
questions.explanation: The page states the new location's 'distance and direction from the original point A is determined by the vector B'.

questions.question: Figure 2.9 labels the translation as [horizontal_factor, vertical_factor] + [x, y]. If a corner of the K is at (2, 1) and the translation is (1.5, 0.5), where does that corner go? Does the K change size?
questions.answer: (3.5, 1.5); no — every point moves by the same vector, so the size and shape are unchanged.
questions.explanation: Add component-wise: 2 + 1.5 = 3.5 and 1 + 0.5 = 1.5. Because all points receive the same displacement, differences between points are preserved.

questions.question: Why does figure 2.8 form a parallelogram, and what does each grey arrow represent?
questions.answer: Because A + B = B + A: chaining B after A and chaining A after B both end at the same point. Each grey arrow is a copy of A or B translated to the head of the other vector.
questions.explanation: The grey arrows in the figure are the chained (translated) copies of the black arrows from p.59's description; commutativity of addition closes the shape.

questions.question: List the elementary geometric operations the page says can be expressed as tensor operations.
questions.answer: Translation, rotation, scaling, skewing, 'and so on'.
questions.explanation: The page names these four explicitly and begins the list of examples with translation; rotation and scaling follow on p.61.

questions.question: Which tensor operation implements translation?
options: Matrix product with a diagonal matrix
Vector addition
Element-wise maximum
Reshaping
questions.answer: Vector addition
questions.explanation: The Translation bullet says 'adding a vector to a point will move this point by a fixed amount in a fixed direction'. A diagonal-matrix product is scaling (p.61); maximum is relu-like clipping; reshaping rearranges coefficients.

questions.question: Explain in your own words how the + b in a Dense layer relates to figure 2.9. Which part of the layer formula would move the point cloud, and which part would change its shape?
questions.answer: + b adds the same vector to every sample's representation, which is a translation of the whole point cloud (figure 2.9 with b as [horizontal_factor, vertical_factor]); matmul(input, W) is what rotates/scales/skews the cloud (p.61).
questions.explanation: The page explains translation; the identification with the bias is spelled out by the authors on p.61 when they call the Dense layer an affine transform.

questions.question: Which matrix rotates a 2-D vector counterclockwise by an angle θ, according to the page?
options: [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]
[[cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ]]
[[sin θ, cos θ], [cos θ, −sin θ]]
[[cos θ, 0], [0, sin θ]]
questions.answer: [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]
questions.explanation: The book gives R = [[cos(theta), -sin(theta)], [sin(theta), cos(theta)]]. The second option is its transpose, which rotates *clockwise* by θ. The third scrambles the entries and is not a rotation. The fourth is diagonal — a scaling, not a rotation.

questions.question: Apply Figure 2.11's scaling matrix [[1, 0], [0, −0.5]] to the point [4, 6]. What do you get, and what happened geometrically?
questions.answer: [4, −3]: the x coordinate is unchanged, the y coordinate is halved and its sign flipped (mirrored across the x-axis).
questions.explanation: Row 1 · [4, 6] = 1·4 + 0·6 = 4; row 2 · [4, 6] = 0·4 + (−0.5)·6 = −3. A diagonal matrix scales each axis independently; the negative factor on y both shrinks and reflects, which is why the K in Figure 2.11 is upside-down and half as tall.

questions.question: What is a 'diagonal matrix', and why does multiplying by one perform scaling rather than rotation?
questions.answer: A matrix whose only non-zero coefficients lie on the diagonal from top left to bottom right. Because the off-diagonal entries are zero, each output coordinate equals its input coordinate times one factor — the axes never mix, so points move along the axes (stretch/shrink) instead of turning.
questions.explanation: The book defines the term in the Scaling bullet. Rotation requires mixing x into y and y into x (the sine terms), which needs non-zero off-diagonal entries.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a linear transform and an affine transform, and say which one a Dense layer without activation computes.
questions.answer: A linear transform is a product with a matrix, x ↦ W @ x; it keeps the origin fixed. An affine transform adds a translation: x ↦ W @ x + b, which can move the origin. A Dense layer without activation computes y = W @ x + b, so it is an affine transform (an 'affine layer').
questions.explanation: The page states that a product with an arbitrary matrix is a linear transform and that an affine transform combines such a product with a vector addition — 'exactly the y = W @ x + b computation implemented by the Dense layer'.

questions.question: Why can the authors say rotation and scaling are linear transforms 'by definition'?
options: Because both are implemented as a product with a matrix, and any matrix product is a linear transform
Because both preserve the lengths of vectors
Because both involve a translation vector
Because both use trigonometric functions
questions.answer: Because both are implemented as a product with a matrix, and any matrix product is a linear transform
questions.explanation: The bullet says 'A product with an arbitrary matrix implements a linear transform' — rotation and scaling are just particular matrices. Scaling does not preserve lengths (so the second option is wrong), neither involves a translation (that would make them affine), and only rotation uses trigonometric functions.

questions.question: Using the rotation matrix with θ = 90°, rotate the point [3, 1]. Then apply an affine transform with the same W and b = [1, 0.25]. Give both results.
questions.explanation: For θ = 90°, cos θ = 0 and sin θ = 1, so R = [[0, −1], [1, 0]]. Row 1: 0·3 + (−1)·1 = −1; row 2: 1·3 + 0·1 = 3. The affine transform then adds the translation vector element-wise — the linear part followed by a translation, exactly as the page defines it.

questions.question: Can you, without looking, (a) write the rotation matrix for an angle θ, (b) sketch what [[1, 0], [0, −0.5]] does to a shape in the first quadrant, and (c) say in one sentence why a Dense layer without activation is 'affine'?
questions.answer: (a) [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]; (b) same width, half the height, flipped below the x-axis; (c) it computes a matrix product (linear transform) plus a bias vector (translation), which is the definition of an affine transform.
questions.explanation: These three items are the page's core content: Figure 2.10's matrix, Figure 2.11's matrix, and the final bullet's identification of y = W @ x + b with an affine transform. If any part is shaky, re-read the corresponding bullet and try the vector_geometry widget.

questions.question: Simplify affine2(affine1(x)) = W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2 into the form W @ x + b, and state W and b.
questions.explanation: Distribute W2 over the sum and regroup the product by associativity: W2 @ (W1 @ x) = (W2 @ W1) @ x. The remaining terms W2 @ b1 + b2 do not depend on x and form the translation. This is exactly the derivation on the page.

questions.question: According to the page, what is a multilayer network made entirely of Dense layers without activation functions equivalent to?
options: A single Dense layer (a linear model in disguise)
A network with the same number of relu layers
A model that cannot be trained by gradient descent
A convolutional network
questions.answer: A single Dense layer (a linear model in disguise)
questions.explanation: Because affine transforms compose into an affine transform, the stack equals one affine layer. The other options are not claimed: relu layers would be strictly more expressive, affine stacks are perfectly trainable (just not more expressive), and convolution is not mentioned here.

questions.question: Why does inserting relu between two Dense layers prevent the collapse into a single affine transform?
questions.answer: relu is not an affine map (it clips negative coordinates to 0, a nonlinear, element-wise operation), so W2 @ relu(W1 @ x + b1) + b2 cannot be rewritten as a single W @ x + b. The distributive step of the proof fails because relu of a sum is not the sum of relus.
questions.explanation: The page says activation functions like relu are needed precisely because they let a chain of Dense layers implement complex nonlinear transformations. Figure 2.13 shows the geometric effect: part of the transformed shape is flattened, which no matrix product plus translation can do.

questions.question: Describe what Figure 2.13 shows and how it differs from Figure 2.12.
questions.answer: Figure 2.12 shows the K after an affine transform W • x + b: a sheared, shifted parallelogram partly below the x-axis. Figure 2.13 applies relu to that result: the portion below the axis is clipped flat onto the axis, giving a straight bottom edge — the transform is no longer affine.
questions.explanation: relu(W • x + b) replaces every negative coordinate by 0, so points under the x-axis move up onto it. The difference between the two figures is exactly the nonlinearity the text says is required.

questions.question: In the crumpled-paper image begun on this page, what do the two sheets of coloured paper represent?
options: The two classes of a classification problem
The training set and the test set
The weights W and the biases b of a layer
The input and output of a single layer
questions.answer: The two classes of a classification problem
questions.explanation: The text says 'each sheet of paper is a class of data in a classification problem' and the crumpled ball is the input data. Train/test splits, layer parameters and layer inputs/outputs are not part of the analogy.

questions.question: Let W1 = [[2, 0], [0, 1]], b1 = [1, 0], W2 = [[0, −1], [1, 0]], b2 = [0, 1]. Compute the collapsed W and b of the composed transform, then verify on x = [1, 1].

The page says a neural network can be interpreted as 'a very complex geometric transformation in a high-dimensional space, implemented via a series of simple steps'. What are the simple steps, and what is the high-dimensional space for the MNIST model of p.52?
questions.answer: The simple steps are the tensor operations of each layer — matmul (rotation/scaling/shear), vector addition (translation), and the activation (relu, a fold). For MNIST the input space is 784-dimensional (one coordinate per pixel); the first Dense layer maps it to a 512-dimensional space and the second to 10 dimensions.
questions.explanation: The paragraph summarizes section 2.3: every tensor operation has a geometric meaning (p.59–61), and layers chain them. The MNIST shapes come from the model in section 2.1 (p.52: Dense(512, activation="relu") followed by Dense(10)).

questions.question: Can you explain to a colleague, in under a minute and without notes, why 'a deep network without activations is a linear model in disguise'?
questions.answer: Each layer is W @ x + b. Feeding one into the next gives W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2 = (W2 @ W1) @ x + (W2 @ b1 + b2), again of the form W @ x + b. Repeat for any depth: still one affine map. An activation such as relu is nonlinear, so it stops this regrouping and lets depth add expressive power.
questions.explanation: If you can reproduce the two-line algebra and name the role of relu, you have the page's main idea. If not, work through the step-by-step derivation in the 'deeper' section and the numerical example.

questions.question: How does the book define a 'manifold', and what does it correspond to in the crumpled-paper image?
questions.answer: A manifold is a continuous surface, like the crumpled sheet of paper. In the image each sheet (each class of data) is a manifold, folded up inside the 3-D space of the ball.
